description: I’m Matías, from Chile: Civil Engineering student at PUC and startup founder. I’m comfortable with Python, web development and ESP32 hardware. I’m interested in astronaut well-being on long missions, especially the psychosocial impact of isolation and communication delays, and in tools that work offline. Looking for teammates in UI/UX design, video/storytelling, psychology or behavioral health, and English pitching. I value research, fast execution and demos that make sense in two minutes.
summary: Tether keeps astronauts close to their families when live calls stop working. Beyond low Earth orbit, communication delay (approximately 8 seconds to the Moon and 3 to 22 minutes to Mars) breaks real-time video calls, and NASA rates behavioral health risk as red for planetary missions. Tether is a crew-facing loop that connects, measures and acts without Earth in the loop: families record "open when..." capsules ahead of time, the astronaut does a 20-second daily check-in (mood, sleep, loneliness, connection to home), a transparent Connection Index compares it with the crew member’s own baseline, and when it dips Tether suggests the right capsule and measures the effect. Heavy news is screened and held so the crew decides when to open it, and ground only sees a consented, non-diagnostic trend. Protecting the crew-family bond is a health measure every long-duration mission will need.
details:
The problem: On the ISS, astronauts have private live video calls with their families. On the Moon and Mars, signal delay makes that impossible, and NASA's evidence shows connection benefits erode at around 8 seconds of delay. NASA already has the pieces (care packages, self-guided behavioral health tools, delay research), but there is no crew-facing layer that monitors connection to home and acts on it without Earth in the loop.

What Tether does (Connect, Measure, Act):
1. Capsule: family members record "open when..." voice or video messages ahead of time (missing home, can't sleep, a hard day). Messages sent during the mission arrive with the real delay of the link.
2. Check-in: the crew member rates mood, sleep, loneliness and connection to home in about 20 seconds a day, plus an optional journal.
3. Index: a Connection Index is computed against each person's own baseline, with the formula visible to the crew, so it is a self-awareness tool and not a black box.
4. Act: when the index dips below baseline, Tether suggests the most fitting capsule and measures the effect on the next check-ins.
Heavy news from home is screened and held so the crew chooses when to open it. Tether first learns from the crew (check-ins, journal, capsule responses) and only then unlocks a conversation mode. Ground receives only an aggregate, consented, non-diagnostic trend, never raw data.

The demo has three views: Family (record a capsule), Crew (check in, open what is waiting, see the Connection Index) and Ground (the consented trend), plus a "Feel the delay" voice echo that lets anyone experience the Moon (8 s) and Mars delay.

What is real vs simulated in the demo: the delay engine, voice echo, capsules, check-in, Connection Index, journal, learning and conversation unlock are working features. Mission history, crew and family data are simulated; heavy-news screening uses a keyword classifier; Mars delay is shortened to 22 seconds for the demo (real: 3 to 22 minutes). Everything runs in the browser and data stays local. Important: Tether is a working proof-of-concept demo, not a deployable system. It runs standalone in the browser and is not integrated with, or ready to plug into, any external system (such as mission communications, crew health platforms or ground networks); that would require separate engineering, security and privacy work.

Benefits and intended impact: protects the crew-family bond when live calls are impossible, gives astronauts autonomous support that does not depend on Earth in real time, and gives ground teams an early, consented signal. Next steps: validate the check-in items with behavioral health experts, connect NASA's red-risk protocols to Tether's alerts to catch crises early, and test it in analog missions (e.g., Antarctic stations or HERA-style habitats).

Tools: web app built with Lovable, running entirely in the browser.
